source: A majority of New York’s gay bars overlap the march route and are clustered on the west side of Manhattan in the West Village, Chelsea, and Hell’s Kitchen.
why: data.csv has one row per ZIP code with only a count of bars (CountBars) and a parade-route flag (ParadeFlag); it has no individual bar locations, no city or borough field, and no way to identify New York’s bars or measure their overlap with the route. Across all ZIP codes, 130 of the 275 bars (47%) fall in a parade-route ZIP, so the majority claim cannot be reproduced from this file.

source: After combining these metrics, it’s no surprise that the west side of Manhattan emerges as a dense gayborhood, but there are also darker areas that stretch into Brooklyn.
why: This describes the shading of the story’s map. data.csv has only ZIP-code identifiers and no city, borough, or neighborhood field, so Manhattan’s west side and Brooklyn cannot be selected from the file.

source: Men dominate the west side, with the highest concentration in Chelsea.
why: Chelsea is a neighborhood label on the story’s map image, not a field in data.csv; the file contains only ZIP codes and no ZIP-to-neighborhood mapping, so this geographic comparison cannot be computed from the file.

source: The strongest cluster appears in Park Slope, Brooklyn, New York’s “lesbian capital.”
why: Park Slope is a neighborhood label on the story’s map image, not a field in data.csv. The file has ZIP-code identifiers only, so the neighborhood cannot be isolated and the smoothed-map cluster cannot be reproduced from the raw ZIP index.

source: For now, same-sex male couples are still concentrated in Midtown, but they are noticeably less visible on the map to the east of the city, especially in the lesbian enclaves of Kirkwood and Decatur, colloquially named “Dick hater.”

source: Boston has some distinct gender patterns, with same-sex male households heavily concentrated in the South End and same-sex female households a little farther out in Jamaica Plain.
